payload.rationale: The event requires the seasonally adjusted U-3 rate for October 2026 (released around Nov 6, 2026) to print at 4.4% or higher. No current data were supplied, and my background knowledge does not reliably extend to the 2026 monthly prints. What I can infer: the labor market softened gradually through 2025 into a range roughly around 4.3–4.6%, with month-to-month moves typically 0.0–0.2 points and the rate often flat. The choice of a 4.3% strike suggests the most recent print near the September 2026 cutoff is close to that level, making this roughly a coin flip on whether the rate sits at/below 4.3% versus 4.4%+ two months later. Structural drift (cooling hiring, immigration-driven labor supply shifts, possible policy easing) is ambiguous in direction over a two-month horizon. Rounding matters: a true rate of 4.35% rounds to 4.4% and resolves Yes, so the effective threshold is the published one-decimal figure. Too high: if the latest print was 4.2–4.3% with a stabilizing or improving trend (e.g., after rate cuts), persistence favors a No outcome, and month-to-month rises of 0.1+ occur only about a third of the time. Too low: if recent prints were already 4.4%+ or trending upward, persistence would favor Yes at 60%+; late-cycle deterioration tends to be sticky. Given genuine ignorance of the anchor value, I center near 0.5.
limitations: No supplied evidence on recent 2026 unemployment prints, revisions, or labor market trend.
Background knowledge of monthly U-3 values in 2026 is unreliable; anchor level inferred only from the contract strike.
Possible data-release disruptions (e.g., government shutdown) could affect timing or settlement, not modeled.
Rounding and seasonal adjustment revisions could shift the published figure by 0.1 point.
